messages.subject: Coastal dolphins, one transect line
parts:
Good day,

I am analysing the data on coastal aerial survey on dolphins. It is a single transect line along the coast with just one observer looking from the surf zone towards the sea.
The animals I am working with are usually in the surf zone or not too far from the coast.

I have different search effort in some areas. Area 1 has 10 surveys (coastal transect line length = 150 km) while Area 2 that is contiguous has just 4 surveys (coastal transect line length just 20 km). The surveys on Area 2 were occasional, depending on the airport that the plane departed from. 

The furthest distance a dolphin was detected was 316 m

I have some questions:
1. Area of survey: Due that the furthest distance that a dolphin was detected is 316 m, can I estimate the area of the survey as [400 m * length of the one transect line]? 
So that would be 0.4 km*150 km

2. Can I do the analysis in distance programme as 1 single area and 1 transect line of different lengths (adapting the survey area according to the length of the transect)? So that will be 0.4*150 km for some transect lines and 0.4*170 km for others.
Or do I have to asses 2 areas as independent with a constant transect length?

3. Can I based the analysis on distance programme as:
-  CDS (Conventional distance sampling); 
- No stratification
- Half normal key function with Cosine series expansion
- Constrains and Diagnostics tabs as default
- Cluster size: use size bias regression method if regression significant... at alpha level 0.15
- Size bias regression method: Regress ln(cluster size) against distance x


Thanks so much in advance,
Have a nice day further
AV

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Coastal dolphins, one transect line
parts:
Alejandra

Before discussing analysis, let me make a few comments about the design.  Your survey design is not the greatest.  Without replicate transects you will not be able to make inference to areas beyond the location you surveyed.  In addition, placing your survey effort parallel to the coast runs the risk of conflating changes in detectability (with increasing distance from transect) with a depth gradient that might influence distribution of dolphins.  It would have been preferable to have placed shorter transects perpendicular to the coast--this way you would have had replicate transects and detectability away from the transect would not have been confounded with potential changes in animal distribution associated with a depth gradient.  I also gather these were one-sided transects (observer looking only out one side of the aircraft--to sea); one-sided transects also create difficulties in determining whether animals close to the transects are included or excluded in your recording.  Challenging.

1--the size of the covered area is the truncation distance (perpendicular distance of farthest detection) times line length.
2--transects in different strata do not need to have equal line lengths
3--if you choose to analyse these data, you would use conventional distance sampling, but you would fit a number of models to the data to determine which model is preferable for the data.

Consult the literature and lecture material available at our website http://distancesampling.org/whatisds.html to get a better perspective on the fundamentals of distance sampling.

Due to aircraft limitations (height and distance from shore) doing the transects perpendicular to the coast was not an option (unfortunately).
I agree that it is going to be challenging, but hopefully we can have an estimate for the area.
